1. True/False/Uncertain and Short Questions
Write whether each statement is true, false or uncertain or answer the question posed. Fully explain your answer, including diagrams where appropriate.

(a) A uniform pricing monopolist has an upward sloping MC curve. Claim: a price ceiling set below the monopoly price will increase welfare relative to the monopoly outcome (assume the monopolist does not shut down).

(b) A large box of paper towels which will last you 2 years is on deep discount at Wal-Mart, saving you $1 per roll. Claim: a rational consumer who has perfectly inelastic demand for paper towels should always purchase this large box instead of paying a higher price for individual paper towel rolls.

(c) In an oligopolistic market with identical firms, the market price is higher when there are two firms in the market than when there are 100 firms in the market.

(d) The government of a developing country is worried about the adverse effect that the high interest rate in the economy has on investment. Claim: Since a low interest rate makes more projects have positive NPV, investment in this economy will increase if the government imposes an interest rate cap.

(e) There are three individuals in society: Bob, Milton and Paul. There are three possible social states which result in different utility levels for the three individuals:

| State | Bob | Milton | Paul |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| A | 12 | 50 | 10 |
| B | 20 | 20 | 20 |
| C | 15 | 15 | 15 |

Are the following True/False/Uncertain? Explain.

(i) No government would choose social state C.

(ii) There is a government election in this society and there are two candidates: a Rawlsian and a Utilitarian government candidates. Claim: In a democratic election (majority win election) a Utilitarian candidate will be elected since more individuals in this society prefer the Utilitarian candidate.

(f) Jon spends his entire budget on espresso and gasoline. You have the following data on his choices:

| Month | Price/gallon gasoline | Price/shot espresso | Gallons purchased | Shots purchased | Total income |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| February | 2 | 1 | 9 | 4 | 22 |
| March | 5/2 | 3/4 | 10 | 8 | 31 |
| April | 3 | 1/2 | 8 | 14 | 31 |

Assume Jon's preferences are monotone, the same over the three months, and that he has no way to save or borrow across periods. Are Jon's choices consistent with utility maximization?

(g) Marco's monthly income is $1000. He spends 40% of his income on food and the rest on buying designer clothes. The City Council thinks it is unfair that people spend more than 35% of their income for food. In order to lower the proportion of income going to food, the City Council gives Marco $200. Claim: given that Marco's income elasticity of food is 2, the City Council accomplishes its goal.

(h) Venus Williams likes both tennis rackets and tennis shoes. She has many of both. Her marginal rate of substitution (MRS) of rackets for shoes is 3, meaning that given the opportunity, she is willing to trade 3 tennis rackets for 1 pair of shoes, or vice versa. Unused rackets and shoes may be returned to the local sporting goods store for a refund. The current price for a racket is $200 and the price for a pair of shoes is $100. Claim: Venus can make herself better off by trading in some tennis rackets in return for some shoes at the market rate.

(i) Suppose that there are two types of drivers: speeders and slowpokes. Speeders are more likely to have accidents, and have expected costs of $5,000 a year in car repair bills. Slowpokes on the other hand have expected costs of only $100 a year. Suppose further that speeders are risk-loving and that slowpokes are risk-averse. Claim: a (risk-neutral) private car insurance company will insure only slowpokes even if there are no asymmetric information or moral hazard problems in this market.

(j) Please outline the pros and cons of the U.S. adopting a tax system with a heavier reliance on a consumption tax.

criteria.label: State whether a price ceiling below the monopoly price increases welfare relative to the monopoly outcome, and explain.
criteria.expected: Uncertain. A binding ceiling can raise output toward the efficient level and improve welfare for some ceiling prices; if set sufficiently low, it can reduce output below the monopoly quantity and lower welfare.
criteria.economic_check: Recognize that a binding ceiling can increase output and reduce monopoly distortion at some levels, but a sufficiently low ceiling can reduce output and welfare; the result is not universally positive.

criteria.label: State whether a rational consumer with perfectly inelastic demand should always buy the discounted two-year box of paper towels, and explain.
criteria.expected: False. The bulk purchase requires a larger upfront payment to obtain future savings. If the opportunity cost of funds is sufficiently high, buying individual rolls over time can be preferable despite the per-roll discount.
criteria.economic_check: Compare the present value of the upfront bulk cost with the stream of individual purchases; a discount does not guarantee savings after accounting for the time value of money.

criteria.label: State whether, in an oligopolistic market with identical firms, price is higher with two firms than with one hundred firms.
criteria.expected: Uncertain. Under Cournot competition, price may be higher with two firms than with one hundred. Under Bertrand competition with identical firms and homogeneous goods, price equals marginal cost with either number of firms. With perfectly elastic demand, price need not vary with firm count.
criteria.economic_check: Recognize that the number-of-firms comparison is model-dependent: Cournot can yield lower prices with more firms, while homogeneous-good Bertrand competition with at least two firms can yield marginal-cost pricing; perfectly elastic demand is another qualification.

criteria.label: State whether imposing an interest-rate cap will increase investment, and explain.
criteria.expected: False. A binding cap below the equilibrium interest rate increases demand for funds and reduces their supply, creating excess demand. The reduced availability of funds can lower investment despite more projects having positive NPV at the capped rate.
criteria.economic_check: A binding cap below the market-clearing rate creates excess demand for funds and reduces the quantity supplied; lower borrowing rates do not ensure greater realized investment when financing is rationed.

criteria.label: State whether no government would choose social state C, and explain.
criteria.expected: True under the standard Pareto-respecting interpretation: B gives Bob, Milton, and Paul utility 20, strictly above C's 15 for each, so C is Pareto dominated. The absolute wording “No government” is not logically guaranteed without a criterion restricting government choices.
criteria.economic_check: Apply Pareto dominance: state B gives each person strictly higher utility than C, so a government whose choice respects unanimous Pareto improvements would not select C.

criteria.label: State whether a Utilitarian candidate will win the majority election because more individuals prefer that candidate, and explain.
criteria.expected: False. A Rawlsian selects B, whose minimum utility is 20; a utilitarian selects A, whose total utility is 72 versus 60 for B. Bob and Paul prefer B to A, while Milton prefers A, so the Rawlsian candidate wins a majority.
criteria.economic_check: Apply the candidate criteria to the given utility table and use pairwise majority voting over the resulting states; do not infer the election result merely from the number of people who prefer a candidate without comparing outcomes.

criteria.label: Determine whether Jon's choices are consistent with utility maximization under the stated assumptions.
criteria.expected: Yes, the choices are consistent. February's bundle costs 22 and neither later bundle is affordable at February prices and income. At March prices, April's bundle costs 8(5/2)+14(3/4)=30.5, within income 31, so choosing March reveals March weakly preferred to April. At April prices, March's bundle costs 10(3)+8(1/2)=34, above income 31. These observations do not create a revealed-preference contradiction.
criteria.economic_check: Use revealed-preference consistency: the April bundle is affordable in March but not chosen, while the March bundle is not affordable in April; neither March nor April is affordable in February. No revealed-preference cycle is forced.

criteria.label: State whether the $200 transfer accomplishes the goal of lowering Marco's food-spending share, given the stated income elasticity.
criteria.expected: False: income-elasticity greater than one implies food expenditure rises proportionally faster than income locally, so its budget share rises rather than falls to35%. The key first-order approximation gives400*(1+2*.20)=560, share46.67%; treating elasticity2 as constant over the full range gives400*1.2^2=576, share48%. Either clearly stated convention or correct qualitative reasoning earns full credit; an exact numeric share is not requested.
criteria.economic_check: Relate income elasticity above one to a rising food expenditure share, distinguishing the expenditure numerator from total income; precise finite-change calculations are not essential to the original true/false task.

criteria.label: State whether Venus can make herself better off by trading in some rackets for shoes at the market rate, and explain.
criteria.expected: True. Venus is willing to give up 3 rackets for one pair of shoes, while the market exchange rate is 1 racket for 2 pairs of shoes (one-half racket per pair). Trading in rackets for shoes at this rate improves her welfare locally.
criteria.economic_check: Compare the consumer's marginal willingness to trade with the market tradeoff; a beneficial exchange is possible when the market offers more shoes per racket surrendered than her stated indifference tradeoff.

criteria.label: State whether a risk-neutral private insurer will insure only slowpokes under the stated conditions, and explain.
criteria.expected: Under the standard voluntary insurance model with actuarially fair or profit-covering premiums and no subsidy, True: a strictly risk-loving driver does not value a reduction in pure income risk at a fair premium (convex utility/Jensen), and an insurer cannot profitably offer a premium sufficiently below fair value. Risk-averse slowpokes may pay at least the fair premium. Accept carefully justified qualifications about offering versus purchasing coverage, but offering a contract alone does not show that speeders buy it.
criteria.economic_check: Distinguish insurer expected-cost pricing from customer demand. Convex utility does not create willingness to pay a positive risk premium for fair pure-risk insurance; do not confuse the ability to offer a contract with actual voluntary insurance uptake.
criteria.source_issue: The source draft confused offering a contract with actual voluntary purchase and rejected the textbook risk-preference implication. The private reference restores the standard actuarial-pricing argument, with justified qualifications accepted.

criteria.label: Outline the pros and cons of the U.S. adopting a tax system with heavier reliance on a consumption tax.
criteria.expected: Possible advantages include encouraging saving by taxing consumption rather than income and potentially supporting capital accumulation and growth. Possible disadvantages include regressivity because lower-income households often consume a larger share of income, as well as transition, compliance, or distributional concerns. Credit other economically sound pros and cons.
criteria.economic_check: Identify at least one plausible saving/incentive or growth advantage and one distributional or implementation disadvantage; qualify claims where outcomes depend on tax design.

**(a) True (with the usual caveat that the ceiling is not set too low).**  
A monopoly restricts output where **MR = MC**, then charges the demand price. Since price exceeds marginal cost at the monopoly quantity, there is deadweight loss. A **binding price ceiling** set **below monopoly price but above the shutdown level** can force the monopolist to expand output. For quantities where the ceiling binds, the firm faces a horizontal demand segment, so **MR = P̄** up to the point where demand intersects the ceiling. With upward-sloping MC, output rises until **MC = P̄**, which moves quantity closer to the efficient level where **P = MC**. Hence welfare rises relative to monopoly, provided the ceiling is not set so low that output falls or shutdown occurs.

**(b) False.**  
Perfectly inelastic demand means the **quantity consumed over the 2 years** does not respond to price. It does **not** imply the consumer should always buy the large box. The rational choice depends on storage costs, liquidity constraints, spoilage risk, moving costs, and the time value of money. If those costs exceed the $1-per-roll saving, buying the large box is not optimal.

**(c) True.**  
In standard oligopoly models with identical firms, more firms usually means more competition and a lower price. For example, in Cournot competition, as the number of firms rises, total output rises and price falls toward marginal cost. So price is typically higher with **2 firms** than with **100 firms**.

**(d) Uncertain.**  
A lower interest rate does make more projects have positive NPV. But an **interest-rate cap** may create **credit shortages**: lenders may supply less credit, banks may ration loans, and risky borrowers may be favored. So even if more projects are profitable on paper, actual investment may fail to rise if firms cannot obtain funds.

**(e)(i) False.**  
A Rawlsian government maximizes the utility of the **worst-off** person. Minimum utilities are: A = 10, B = 20, C = 15. So a Rawlsian government would choose **B**, not C. But some governments might choose **C**—for example, one that values equality strongly but not strictly by the Rawlsian criterion, or one with other political objectives. So it is false that **no** government would choose C.

**(e)(ii) False.**  
A utilitarian chooses the state with highest total utility:  
- A: 72  
- B: 60  
- C: 45  
So the utilitarian candidate favors **A**. A Rawlsian favors **B**. Individual preferences between A and B:  
- Bob: prefers **B** (20 > 12)  
- Milton: prefers **A** (50 > 20)  
- Paul: prefers **B** (20 > 10)  
Thus **2 out of 3** prefer the Rawlsian outcome, so the **Rawlsian candidate wins**.

**(f) No, not consistent with utility maximization.**  
Use revealed preference.  
- February bundle: (9,4), income 22. At March prices, cost = 
  
  	(5/2)9 + (3/4)4 = 22.5 + 3 = 25.5 < 31.  
So in March, Jon could have afforded February’s bundle but chose March bundle (10,8). Therefore March is directly revealed preferred to February.
- March bundle at April prices costs 
  
  	3(10) + (1/2)8 = 30 + 4 = 34 > 31,  
so not affordable in April.
- April bundle at February prices costs 
  
  	2(8) + 1(14) = 30 > 22,  
not affordable in February.
- April bundle at March prices costs 
  
  	(5/2)8 + (3/4)14 = 20 + 10.5 = 30.5 < 31.  
So in March, Jon could have afforded April’s bundle but chose March bundle. Hence March is directly revealed preferred to April.

Now compare February and April: at April prices, February costs 3(9)+0.5(4)=29 < 31, so April is directly revealed preferred to February too. No contradiction arises yet. But February bundle has **more gasoline and less espresso** than April; with monotone preferences this is possible. Thus data **are consistent** with utility maximization.

**Correction:** Therefore the answer is **Yes, consistent**.

**(g) False.**  
Income rises from 1000 to 1200, a **20% increase**. With income elasticity of demand for food = 2, food expenditure/quantity demanded rises by about **40%**. Initially food spending is 40% of 1000 = **400**. After the transfer, food spending rises to about **560**. As a share of new income, that is **560/1200 = 46.7%**, which is **higher**, not lower than 35%.

**(h) True.**  
Her MRS is 3 rackets for 1 pair of shoes, so she values 1 pair of shoes as much as 3 rackets. Market tradeoff is only **2 rackets per pair of shoes** ($200 each racket, $100 shoes). Since she is willing to give up 3 rackets for shoes but market requires only 2, shoes are relatively cheap for her. She can trade in some rackets for shoes and become better off.

**(i) False.**  
With no asymmetric information or moral hazard, a risk-neutral insurer can offer actuarially fair or profitable contracts to both types. Risk-averse slowpokes certainly demand insurance. Risk-loving speeders may prefer not to insure at actuarially fair prices, but the claim says the company **will insure only slowpokes**. That need not be true: if speeders are willing to buy some contract at a premium above expected cost, the insurer would also insure them.

**(j) Heavier reliance on consumption taxation: pros and cons**

**Pros**
- Encourages saving and investment relative to income taxation.  
- Broader tax base can raise revenue efficiently.  
- Can reduce distortions to work, saving, and capital formation.  
- Harder to avoid than some income taxes if collected at point of sale/VAT stages.

**Cons**
- Usually **regressive**: lower-income households spend a larger share of income on consumption.  
- Can reduce purchasing power, especially for necessities.  
- Transitional unfairness: people who already paid income tax on saved earnings may be taxed again when spending.  
- Administrative/political issues in exempting essentials or compensating poorer households.  
- May hurt sectors sensitive to consumer spending in the short run.

## Answers to Microeconomics Questions

### (a) Price Ceiling and Monopoly Welfare
**Answer: TRUE**

A price ceiling below the monopoly price can increase welfare. Under monopoly, the firm restricts output where MR = MC, creating deadweight loss. A binding price ceiling forces the firm to act as a price-taker at the ceiling price. If set appropriately (between competitive and monopoly prices), the firm will increase output to where P = MC, eliminating the deadweight loss from monopoly underproduction. Consumer surplus increases substantially, and while producer surplus falls, the net welfare gain is positive. The key assumption that the firm doesn't shut down ensures output remains positive.

### (b) Perfectly Inelastic Demand and Bulk Purchase
**Answer: FALSE**

Perfectly inelastic demand means quantity demanded doesn't respond to price changes. However, this doesn't mean the consumer is indifferent about *when* to purchase or in what quantities. A rational consumer considers storage costs, shelf life, and the time value of money. Even with perfectly inelastic demand for the total quantity needed over 2 years, the consumer should compare: (1) the present value of buying in bulk now versus (2) buying smaller quantities over time. If storage costs or interest rates are high, buying individual rolls at higher prices may be rational. The discount must exceed these carrying costs.

### (c) Oligopoly Price and Number of Firms
**Answer: TRUE**

With identical firms in oligopoly, as the number of firms increases, market price falls toward the competitive level. With 2 firms (duopoly), firms have significant market power and can sustain higher prices through implicit collusion or strategic interaction. With 100 firms, each firm's individual output has negligible effect on market price, pushing behavior toward perfect competition where P = MC. This follows from oligopoly theory: fewer firms → higher prices.

### (d) Interest Rate Cap and Investment
**Answer: FALSE**

While a lower interest rate makes more projects have positive NPV, an interest rate cap creates a binding constraint that prevents the market from clearing. At the artificially low rate, demand for credit exceeds supply. Banks ration credit, and many projects that appear profitable at the capped rate cannot obtain financing. Additionally, lenders reduce supply of credit, and investment projects that would have been funded at market rates may not be approved. The cap distorts investment allocation and typically reduces total investment below the market outcome.

### (e) Social Welfare Comparisons

**(i) FALSE**

A government could choose state C. While state C is Pareto-dominated by both A and B (everyone is worse off than in B), a Rawlsian government maximizing the minimum utility would prefer C (minimum = 15) over A (minimum = 10). A Rawlsian would actually prefer C to A, and might prefer C to B depending on how much weight is placed on equality versus total welfare.

**(ii) FALSE**

The Utilitarian candidate prefers state A (total utility = 72) over state C (total utility = 45). The Rawlsian candidate prefers state C (minimum = 15) over state A (minimum = 10). In a majority vote:
- Bob prefers B to A (20 > 12) and B to C (20 > 15)
- Milton prefers A to B (50 > 20) and A to C (50 > 15)
- Paul prefers B to A (20 > 10) and B to C (20 > 15)

Majority (Bob and Paul) prefer B. The Utilitarian candidate loses to a candidate proposing state B.

### (f) Revealed Preference Consistency
**Answer: NO**

Checking revealed preference violations:
- February bundle: (9G, 4E) costs $22 ✓
- March bundle: (10G, 8E) at Feb prices = $9(2) + 8(1) = $26 > $22, so Feb bundle was affordable but not chosen
- March bundle costs $31 ✓
- April bundle: (8G, 14E) at March prices = 8(2.5) + 14(0.75) = $31 ✓
- March bundle at April prices = 10(3) + 8(0.5) = $34 > $31, so April bundle was affordable but not chosen

The March bundle was revealed preferred to February's, but April's bundle was revealed preferred to March's. However, checking February vs. April: February bundle at April prices = 9(3) + 4(0.5) = $29 < $31. So April bundle was affordable in February but not chosen, while February bundle was affordable in April but not chosen. This violates the weak axiom of revealed preference.

### (g) Income Elasticity and Food Spending
**Answer: FALSE**

Initially: Marco spends $400 on food (40% of $1000). After receiving $200, his income is $1200. With income elasticity of 2, a 20% income increase (200/1000) causes a 40% increase in food quantity demanded. If food prices are constant, food spending increases by 40%: $400 × 1.4 = $560. As a percentage of new income: $560/$1200 = 46.7%, which exceeds the 35% target. The goal is not accomplished.

### (h) MRS and Market Trade
**Answer: TRUE**

Venus's MRS = 3 means she values 1 shoe at 3 rackets. The market price ratio is $200/$100 = 2 rackets per shoe. Since she values shoes more highly (3 rackets) than the market price (2 rackets), she should trade rackets for shoes. By trading 2 rackets for 1 shoe at market prices, she gets a shoe worth 3 rackets to her, gaining utility.

### (i) Insurance Market Segmentation
**Answer: TRUE**

Even without asymmetric information or moral hazard, the insurance company will insure only slowpokes. Speeders are risk-loving, so they don't value insurance (they prefer the gamble). Slowpokes are risk-averse and willing to pay a premium above expected costs for insurance. The company can profitably insure risk-averse slowpokes at a premium above $100. Speeders won't purchase insurance at any actuarially fair or profitable premium because they prefer risk.

### (j) Consumption Tax Pros and Cons

**Pros:**
- Encourages saving and capital accumulation, potentially increasing long-term growth
- Avoids double taxation of savings (income tax taxes both earning and returns)
- Simpler to administer than income tax (fewer deductions)
- Reduces tax avoidance through income shifting
- Encourages work effort (no tax on returns to labor savings)

**Cons:**
- Regressive: lower-income households spend larger share of income on consumption
- Transition issues: existing savers face retroactive taxation
- Requires high rates to generate equivalent revenue, creating large deadweight loss
- Difficult to implement with existing income tax system
- May increase inequality without offsetting transfers
- Politically difficult due to perceived unfairness to current retirees

**Answer: False**

A rational consumer with perfectly inelastic demand should not necessarily always purchase the discounted bulk box. The consumer must compare: (1) the present value of savings from the bulk discount against (2) the opportunity cost of paying the lump sum upfront and (3) storage costs or spoilage risk over 2 years. If the consumer faces liquidity constraints or has better uses for that capital, the bulk purchase may not maximize utility despite the per-unit savings. Rationality requires comparing total lifetime costs, not just per-unit prices.

**Answer: True**

- **Uncertain**. While lower interest rates generally make more projects have positive NPV, the actual impact depends on other factors like project availability, risk, and economic conditions. Imposing an interest rate cap might help, but it could also distort credit markets.

**(e)** Social states and government preferences.

- **False**. State C offers equal utility (15) to all individuals, which might be preferred for fairness or stability, so a government might choose it.

(ii) Utilitarian candidate in majority voting.
- **Uncertain**. The utilitarian candidate aims to maximize total utility, which is highest in state B (total utility 60). However, whether they win depends on voters' preferences, not just the aggregate utility.

**(f)** Jon's choices over three months.

**(g)** Marco's income and food expenditure.

**(j)** Pros and cons of a consumption tax.
- **Pros**: Encourages saving and investment, broadens the tax base, and can be less distortive.

With a uniform pricing monopolist and upward-sloping MC, a price ceiling set **below** the monopoly price reduces the price the firm receives. That lowers the quantity supplied (since the firm produces where **MR = MC**, but the ceiling constrains the price). Welfare relative to the monopoly outcome depends on whether the ceiling reduces deadweight loss enough to offset the loss in producer surplus and any additional distortion. In the standard monopoly model, a binding price ceiling below the monopoly price **typically increases consumer surplus but reduces producer surplus and can reduce total surplus**; with upward-sloping MC, the effect is not guaranteed to be welfare-improving. Since the claim says it **will** increase welfare, it is **false**.

### (b) **True/False/Uncertain: False**
If demand is perfectly inelastic, the consumer buys the same quantity regardless of price. But the claim says the consumer should **always** buy the discounted large box instead of higher-priced rolls. That is only true if the **effective per-unit price** of the box is lower (it is: $1 saved per roll). However, “perfectly inelastic demand” means quantity is fixed, not that the consumer must choose the cheaper package. If the box and rolls are perfect substitutes in consumption (same “rolls” utility), then yes they would choose the cheaper option. But the statement says “always” without specifying substitutability/packaging constraints. In general, packaging could affect utility (e.g., storage, convenience, minimum purchase sizes). Therefore the blanket claim is **false/uncertain**; given typical textbook assumptions of perfect substitutability, it would be true, but the question’s wording makes it **false**.

### (c) **True/False/Uncertain: False**
With identical firms, more firms usually increases competition and drives price **down** (e.g., Bertrand competition with homogeneous goods: price tends toward marginal cost as the number of firms rises). So the claim that price is higher with **2** firms than with **100** firms is **false**.

### (d) **True/False/Uncertain: False**
A lower interest rate can increase the NPV of projects, but an **interest rate cap** may also cause credit rationing, reduce supply of loanable funds, and raise risk premia. The statement claims investment will increase **because** more projects have positive NPV. That ignores general-equilibrium/credit-market effects. So the claim is **false**.

MRS of rackets for shoes = 3 means she is willing to give up 3 rackets for 1 shoe (at the margin). Market trade rate: price ratio p_r/p_s = 200/100 = 2 rackets per shoe.
Since her MRS (3) > market rate (2), she values a shoe more relative to rackets than the market does. Therefore she can improve welfare by trading 3 rackets for 1 shoe at her preferred rate; at the market rate she can get **more shoes per racket given up** than she would require. Hence she can be better off by trading some rackets for shoes.

Expected repair costs: speeders $5000, slowpokes $100.
A risk-neutral insurer sets premiums based on expected costs and must consider adverse selection. Even with no asymmetric information/moral hazard, the insurer can’t force types to reveal; but if both types exist and the insurer offers a contract, both types will compare expected utility.
Risk-loving speeders may be willing to pay for insurance even if it is actuarially fair or even if it reduces their expected utility, depending on contract structure. The claim that the insurer will insure only slowpokes “even if there are no asymmetric information” is incorrect: without asymmetric information, the insurer can offer a single contract and both types will participate if it is acceptable. Therefore the claim is **false**.

**Pros**
- Often more efficient than income taxes: can reduce distortions to saving/investment.
- Broad base can raise revenue with relatively lower rates.
- Easier to administer than complex income tax systems.

**Cons**
- Regressive in practice: lower-income households spend a larger share of income.
- Can increase cost of living; may require rebates/exemptions.
- May shift tax burden toward consumption and away from capital income.
- Compliance and enforcement issues (especially with VAT) can be significant.

Even with **perfectly inelastic demand**, a rational consumer should buy the cheaper option **only if it is feasible and truly equivalent in quantity**. More directly: with perfectly inelastic demand, the consumer’s quantity is fixed, but the **choice among bundles** depends on the **effective per-roll price** and any constraints. ### (c) **Uncertain**
In oligopoly with identical firms, the relationship between the number of firms and price depends on the **strategic interaction** (Cournot vs Bertrand), **entry/exit**, and whether firms compete in prices or quantities.

- Under **Bertrand with homogeneous goods**, price can be driven to marginal cost even with few firms.

So the statement “price is higher with two firms than with 100 firms” is **not universally true** across oligopoly models. Therefore **uncertain**.

### (a) False
A ceiling below the monopoly price does not necessarily raise welfare. With upward-sloping MC, a binding ceiling can force the monopolist to expand output beyond the efficient quantity, where **MC exceeds willingness to pay**. The resulting extra units create deadweight loss. A ceiling set between the monopoly and competitive prices can instead raise output toward the efficient level, so the effect depends on its level. The assumption that the firm does not shut down does not guarantee a welfare gain.

### (b) False
Perfectly inelastic demand means the quantity desired does not respond to price; it does not mean buying a two-year supply is always best. The consumer should compare the $1-per-roll saving with storage costs, the cost of tying up money, spoilage or damage, and the value of flexibility. If these costs are negligible, buying the discounted box is advantageous; “always” is too strong.

### (c) Uncertain
The claim holds in standard models such as Cournot competition with identical firms: more firms generally increase total output and lower price toward marginal cost. But “oligopolistic market” alone does not specify firms’ conduct, demand, costs, or entry conditions, so the result is not guaranteed.

### (d) False
A binding interest-rate cap below the market-clearing rate creates excess demand for credit. Lenders may ration loans, and projects with positive NPV may not obtain financing. A lower posted rate therefore does not ensure that investment rises; it may reduce the supply or allocation of funds.

### (e)
**(i) Uncertain.** Under utilitarianism, totals are A = 72, B = 60, C = 45, so C is not chosen. Under a Rawlsian maximin rule, the minimum utilities are A = 10, B = 20, C = 15, so B is chosen. But other social objectives or constraints could select C; no social welfare rule is specified.

**(ii) False.** A Rawlsian candidate chooses B (highest minimum utility); a utilitarian chooses A (highest total utility). Bob prefers B to A, while Milton and Paul prefer A to B. Thus only two of three prefer the utilitarian candidate, so that candidate wins by majority—**if** voters choose according to their own listed utilities and the candidates’ policies are exactly these states. The claim’s conclusion is true under those assumptions, but the stated reason “more individuals … prefer” is correct. **True under the natural voting interpretation.**

### (f) No: choices violate GARP
February’s bundle costs $22 at February prices. At March prices it costs $25.50, so March’s chosen bundle is affordable in February, but February’s bundle is not affordable in March (it costs $26). Thus February is directly revealed preferred to March. March’s bundle costs $31 at April prices, exactly April’s budget, so April is directly revealed preferred to March. More decisively, April’s bundle costs $38 at February prices, so it is not affordable then; March’s bundle costs $31 at February prices, also unaffordable. The revealed-preference comparisons do not produce a contradiction: **the data are consistent with utility maximization**. (Monotonicity is compatible with these choices.)

Food spending is initially $400. A 20% income increase, with food income elasticity 2, implies food expenditure rises by approximately 40% to $560 (using the elasticity as the stated proportional response). Venus is willing to give up 3 rackets for one pair of shoes, so her MRS implies shoes are worth 3 rackets to her, while the market requires only 0.5 racket per pair. This wording is ambiguous about the direction of the MRS: if she truly values a shoe at 3 rackets, she should trade rackets for shoes and can gain. A rational consumer buys the bulk package only if its total benefit exceeds these costs.

A consumption tax can encourage saving because returns to saving are not taxed until spent; it may also broaden the tax base and raise revenue with relatively little distortion to work and investment decisions.
